ruled_out.assertion: LIMIT/OFFSET spliced into the recent-notes statement is SQL injection
ruled_out.killed_by: hearth-sinatra/app.rb:106-109 - page is params.fetch('page','1').to_i and limit is Integer(...), clamped to 1..100, so only Ruby Integers reach the interpolation.

ruled_out.assertion: State-changing POST routes are CSRF-able because no anti-forgery token exists in any form
ruled_out.killed_by: hearth-sinatra/app.rb:18 - the session cookie is set with same_site: :lax and every state-changing route is a POST, so the browser does not attach hearth.sid to a cross-site submission (WEB-15's own exculpation).

ruled_out.assertion: Login does not regenerate the session identifier, so the app is open to session fixation
ruled_out.killed_by: hearth-sinatra/app.rb:16 - enable :sessions uses Rack::Session::Cookie, which keeps the state in the cookie itself; the post-login uid is written into a freshly signed cookie the attacker's fixed copy never receives.

ruled_out.assertion: The flash banner is rendered raw with <%== notice %> and is an XSS sink
ruled_out.killed_by: hearth-sinatra/app.rb:47 - take_notice returns NOTICES[key.to_sym], a lookup in the frozen literal table at app.rb:25-32; a session value that is not a key yields nil.

ruled_out.assertion: cors({origin: true, credentials: true}) reflects any Origin with credentials
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsedeck-graphql/src/server.js:33 and :82 - requireAllowedOrigin is mounted ahead of the cors middleware on /graphql and 403s any Origin not in config.cors.allowedOrigins, preflight included.

ruled_out.assertion: windowDays and limit are interpolated into the bucket query, so eventBuckets is injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsedeck-graphql/src/schema.graphql:44 - both are declared Int!, so GraphQL coerces them to numbers and rejects non-integers before the resolver runs; Math.min on line 25-26 keeps them numeric.

ruled_out.assertion: The slow-query log line lets an attacker forge log records through the injected search term
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsedeck-graphql/src/db.js:26 - .replace(/\s+/g, ' ') collapses every whitespace run, CR and LF included, before the string reaches console.warn.

ruled_out.assertion: analytics.publishableKey committed in config/default.json is an exposed secret
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsedeck-graphql/src/analytics.js:13-17 - authentication of a batch is the HMAC from process.env.ANALYTICS_SECRET, and signBatch throws when it is unset; the key only names the workspace.

ruled_out.assertion: No depth or complexity limit on the GraphQL endpoint permits a recursive query bomb
ruled_out.killed_by: pulsedeck-graphql/src/schema.graphql:8-48 - no type in the schema has a field of an object type, so no query can nest beyond depth two and there is no cycle to recurse on.

ruled_out.assertion: The mail store bucket policy grants s3:GetObject to Principal '*'
ruled_out.killed_by: mailroom-lambda/template.yaml:70-72 - the statement carries Condition StringEquals aws:PrincipalOrgID: !Ref OrgId, which is the account-narrowing condition INF-02 names as the exculpation.

ruled_out.assertion: A signing secret is committed in the webhook test suite
ruled_out.killed_by: mailroom-lambda/tests/test_webhook.py:10-13 - the value is the carrier's published sandbox secret, paired with the EXAMPLE_SIGNATURE_HEADER in the integration guide, and the comment states production uses MAILROOM_SIGNING_SECRET instead.

ruled_out.assertion: CORS allowedOrigins is '*' on the order API
ruled_out.killed_by: orderbook-spring/src/main/resources/application.yml:5 and :63-67 - the wildcard lives in the document activated on-profile: local, while spring.profiles.active is prod, whose document lists two explicit origins on lines 52-55.

ruled_out.assertion: findByStatus splices the status into the SQL string, so it is injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: orderbook-spring/src/main/java/io/orderbook/web/OrderController.java:46 - the parameter is bound as an OrderStatus, so Spring rejects anything that is not one of the seven constants in model/OrderStatus.java, and .name() can only return one of those.

ruled_out.assertion: findRecent concatenates the LIMIT, so the recent and export routes are injectable
ruled_out.killed_by: orderbook-spring/src/main/java/io/orderbook/web/OrderController.java:53 - the value is an int bound by Spring and clamped with Math.min(limit, 200); the export caller passes the int from orderbook.export.max-rows.

ruled_out.assertion: csrf().disable() leaves the API open to cross-site request forgery
ruled_out.killed_by: orderbook-spring/src/main/java/io/orderbook/web/SecurityConfig.java:66 - SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS, and the only credential any handler reads is the Authorization header (SecurityConfig.java:78); no cookie the browser attaches on its own authorizes anything.

ruled_out.assertion: anchorFor turns a message-supplied target into a CSS selector
ruled_out.killed_by: tabsnap-extension/lib/allowlist.js:9-16 - CLIP_TARGETS is a fixed six-entry map and an unknown key yields undefined, which content.js:7-9 turns into document.body; the message value never reaches querySelector.

ruled_out.assertion: The popup writes the clip title and URL into innerHTML
ruled_out.killed_by: tabsnap-extension/popup.js:24 - both interpolations are wrapped in escapeHtml (defined at lines 5-12), and markdownLite at lines 69-74 likewise escapes before adding markup, which is the correct order.

ruled_out.assertion: The pprof/expvar debug port is reachable from anywhere in the cluster
ruled_out.killed_by: ledger-k8s/templates/networkpolicy.yaml:23-25 - the only ingress rule admits {{ .Values.service.port }} (8080) and nothing else, and the Ingress at templates/ingress.yaml:29 also forwards only to that port.

ruled_out.assertion: The ledger ServiceAccount auto-mounts its API token into the pod
ruled_out.killed_by: ledger-k8s/templates/deployment.yaml:31 - the pod spec sets automountServiceAccountToken: false, which overrides the ServiceAccount default for this workload.

ruled_out.assertion: templates/secret.yaml commits real credentials in base64
ruled_out.killed_by: ledger-k8s/templates/secret.yaml:16-17 decoded - the two values are the ASCII strings 'placeholder-replaced-by-vault-injector' and 'not-a-real-token-see-vault-path', matching the annotation at line 12 that says the object is checked in for its shape only.

ruled_out.assertion: The NetworkPolicy lists namespaceSelector and podSelector as two peers, so any pod in the platform namespace and any gateway pod anywhere is admitted
ruled_out.killed_by: ledger-k8s/templates/networkpolicy.yaml:20 - podSelector is indented as a sibling key inside the same list item that opens at line 17, so the two selectors are ANDed exactly as the comment claims.

findings.title: SQL injection in note search
findings.evidence: app.rb:116 passes params[:q] straight into DB.search; lib/db.rb:41-48 builds the statement by interpolation: "... AND (title LIKE '%#{term}%' OR body LIKE '%#{term}%')" and calls handle.execute with no bind list. The sibling helpers in the same file (user_by_email:19, note:23, save_note:52) all use ? placeholders, so the interpolation is the exception, not the house style.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user can terminate the string literal and append arbitrary SQL to a SELECT that already runs with full database rights: UNION SELECT over users reads every account's email, role and bcrypt password_digest, and over notes reads every other user's note bodies, defeating the owner_id scoping the rest of the module enforces.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: "... AND (title LIKE ? OR body LIKE ?)" with ["%#{term}%", "%#{term}%"], and bind owner_id on the same statement instead of interpolating it.

findings.title: Session signing secret hard-coded in the application source
findings.evidence: set :session_secret, 'hearth-notes-session-secret-v2' with no ENV fallback. Sessions are Rack::Session::Cookie (enable :sessions, app.rb:16), which signs the serialized session with that value; session[:uid] (app.rb:92) is the only thing current_user consults (app.rb:36-39) and role is read from the row it loads.
findings.impact: Anyone who can read this file - the repository, the image, any self-hosted copy - can mint a cookie carrying an arbitrary uid and authenticate as any user, including one whose role is 'admin', which is the whole gate on /admin/* (app.rb:61-64). The cookie payload is signed but not encrypted, so session contents are also readable.
findings.recommendation: Load the secret from the environment and fail to boot when it is absent; rotate the current value, which must be treated as compromised; generate at least 64 bytes from a CSPRNG.

findings.title: Path traversal in the attachment download route
findings.evidence: name = params[:name].to_s (app.rb:149) is checked only for emptiness and then File.join(Attachments::ROOT, name) is handed to send_file. There is no canonicalisation, no basename extraction and no check that the resolved path stays under Attachments::ROOT. File.join does not normalise '..' segments and Sinatra's send_file does not confine reads to public_folder.
findings.impact: Any logged-in user reads arbitrary files the application process can open - ../../data/hearth.db (the whole notes database and every bcrypt digest), the application source including the session secret at app.rb:17, or any file on the host.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the candidate with File.expand_path and reject it unless it starts with File.expand_path(Attachments::ROOT) + File::SEPARATOR; better, look the attachment up by a database row the caller owns and never accept a filesystem path from the client.

findings.title: Attachment download is not scoped to the owner
findings.evidence: Attachments.store writes to File.join(ROOT, owner_id.to_s, digest+ext) (lib/attachments.rb:15), so files are partitioned per owner on disk, but the download route joins ROOT with the client-supplied name directly and never inserts current_user['id']. Every other data path in the app scopes on owner (DB.note:22, DB.recent_notes:31, DB.save_note:51).
findings.impact: A logged-in user who learns or guesses another user's directory and content digest - or simply enumerates - reads other users' uploaded files. Fixing only the traversal above leaves this open, because '2/<digest>.pdf' contains no '..' at all.
findings.recommendation: Build the path as File.join(ROOT, current_user['id'].to_s, basename) and serve only entries recorded against that owner.

findings.title: Open redirect on the login form's next parameter
findings.evidence: destination = params[:next].to_s; redirect destination.empty? ? '/notes' : destination. The value is round-tripped through the hidden field rendered at app.rb:74 and is never validated as a relative path or matched against an allowlist of hosts.
findings.impact: A crafted /login?next=https://attacker.example lands the user on an attacker page immediately after a successful authentication, which is the moment a credential-phishing replica is most convincing; it also lets a phishing link carry this application's own domain.
findings.recommendation: Accept only paths: reject the value unless it starts with a single '/' and not '//' (and not a scheme), else fall back to '/notes'.

findings.title: Note bodies rendered as Markdown with inline HTML enabled and emitted unescaped
findings.evidence: Redcarpet::Render::HTML is constructed with filter_html: false and escape_html: false (lib/markdown.rb:19-20), and the result is written with the raw tag <%== body_html %> in views/note.erb:6 while the rest of the template uses the escaping <%= %>. No sanitiser runs between the two.
findings.impact: Script in a note body executes in the reader's session. Within this tree the only principal who can write a note is its owner (DB.save_note scopes on owner_id, and the SameSite=Lax session cookie blocks a cross-site POST), so the second principal cannot be named from what was given and the realistic impact is self-XSS or a payload arriving through a future import/sharing path. Reported at low for that reason.
findings.recommendation: Run the rendered HTML through an allowlist sanitiser (e.g. Sanitize) after Redcarpet, or set filter_html: true / escape_html: true and whitelist the handful of tags people actually paste.

findings.title: Shell command built by interpolation in the legacy archive importer
findings.evidence: system("tar xf #{archive_path} -C #{dest}") - a single string, so it is run through the shell, with archive_path interpolated. grep across the tree finds no caller: the only occurrence of legacy_import is its own definition at lib/attachments.rb:26.
findings.impact: No route reaches it today, so it is not exploitable as shipped; the moment any handler wires a user-supplied path into it, an argument containing ; or $( ) executes commands as the application user. It is retained code with a live sink, which the comment at lines 24-25 says is kept only until a migration finishes.
findings.recommendation: Delete it, or at minimum call the argv form: system('tar', 'xf', archive_path, '-C', dest), which never involves a shell.

findings.title: Session cookie is not marked Secure
findings.evidence: set :sessions, key: 'hearth.sid', httponly: true, same_site: :lax - httponly and same_site are set explicitly and secure is absent, so the cookie is sent over plaintext HTTP as well. Nothing else in the tree (config.ru, app.rb) forces TLS or emits HSTS.
findings.impact: On any deployment reachable over http, a network observer captures the signed session cookie and replays it; because the cookie carries the whole session, capture is sufficient for full account takeover.
findings.recommendation: Add secure: true to the same options hash (gated on the environment if a plaintext local run is needed) and redirect http to https at the front door.

findings.title: Authentication falls back to an unverified token when verification fails
findings.evidence: attachPrincipal wraps verify(raw) in try/catch and, on any exception, sets req.principal = identify(raw). identify (src/auth/token.js:30-34) is jwt.decode, which the file's own comment says 'skips the exp check that verify() would trip on' - but jwt.decode checks nothing at all: no signature, no algorithm, no issuer. requireSession (server.js:61) then admits the request and the resolver context is built from that payload (server.js:86).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller sends a self-made JWT with any sub, org and role - no signing key needed, since the signature is never examined - and every resolver treats it as that principal. ctx.user.org is the only tenant boundary in users.js and reports.js, so this reads and writes any organisation's members and reports (orgMembers, exportReport, deactivateUser, saveReport).
findings.recommendation: Remove the fallback: a failed verify is a 401. If a grace period for a just-expired access token is genuinely required, call jwt.verify with ignoreExpiration only for that one case, keep signature/issuer/algorithm checks, and bound it by a short window against the exp claim.

findings.title: JWT signing key falls back to a value committed in the source
findings.evidence: const SECRET = process.env.JWT_SECRET || 'pulsedeck-local-signing-key'; used both to sign (issue, line 11) and to verify (verify, line 19). Nothing in the tree asserts JWT_SECRET is present - contrast analytics.js:14-16, which throws when ANALYTICS_SECRET is missing.
findings.impact: If JWT_SECRET is unset in any environment the service still starts and happily verifies tokens signed with a key printed in the repository, so anyone can mint a valid token for any org and role. The failure is silent: there is no log line and no start-up check.
findings.recommendation: Drop the literal and throw at module load when process.env.JWT_SECRET is absent, mirroring the pattern already used in analytics.js.

findings.title: SQL injection in the report search resolver
findings.evidence: args.term is declared String! in schema.graphql:46 - an arbitrary string, not a constrained scalar - and is interpolated into the statement: "AND (title ILIKE '%${args.term}%' OR description ILIKE '%${args.term}%')". org_id on the line above is bound as $1, which shows the parameterised form was available and was not used for term.
findings.impact: A caller closes the quote and appends arbitrary SQL to a query that runs with the application's full database rights; the org_id = $1 predicate is trivially neutralised with an OR or a UNION, so this reads every organisation's reports and any other table the role can see. The literal also breaks on a plain apostrophe, so it is reachable by accident as well as on purpose.
findings.recommendation: Pass the pattern as a parameter: WHERE org_id = $1 AND (title ILIKE $2 OR description ILIKE $2) with query(sql, [ctx.user.org, `%${args.term}%`]).

findings.title: Password reset tokens returned to every member of the organisation
findings.evidence: MEMBER_COLUMNS (users.js:5-7) selects reset_token, toUser maps it onto resetToken (users.js:18), the schema publishes it as User.resetToken (schema.graphql:14), and Query.orgMembers (users.js:32-38) returns the whole list to any caller whose ctx.user.org matches - with no role condition. The comment at users.js:9-10 says the console only needs to show a 'reset pending' pill.
findings.impact: Any member - including a VIEWER - queries { orgMembers { email resetToken } } and receives live password-reset tokens for their colleagues, including owners, which is a direct account-takeover path inside the tenant. The same field is also returned by me and by inviteUser.
findings.recommendation: Remove resetToken from the schema and from MEMBER_COLUMNS; if the pill is needed, expose a boolean resetPending computed server-side (reset_token IS NOT NULL).

findings.title: No function-level authorization on the user-administration mutations
findings.evidence: deactivateUser and inviteUser read ctx.user.org and ctx.user.id but never inspect ctx.user.role, and there is no directive, wrapper or middleware between expressMiddleware (server.js:85) and the resolver map (server.js:20-23). The comment at users.js:52-53 states the restriction outright: 'The console only renders the deactivate control for owners' - that is a UI-rendering decision, not a server-side check.
findings.impact: Any authenticated member of an organisation can deactivate any other member of that organisation, owners included, and can create new MEMBER/VIEWER accounts under it. The role claim is carried on the token and simply never consulted.
findings.recommendation: Enforce the role in the resolver (or in a shared wrapper applied to the Mutation map): reject unless ctx.user.role is the owner/admin role, and cover it with a test that calls the mutation as a VIEWER.

findings.title: Database TLS certificate verification disabled
findings.evidence: ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false } on the pg Pool, with the comment explaining that the provider's internal CA is not in the container trust store. No ca: option is supplied anywhere, so the connection is encrypted but the peer is unauthenticated.
findings.impact: Any party able to intercept or redirect the route to pulsedeck-primary.internal presents its own certificate and is accepted, yielding the credentials in PGUSER/PGPASSWORD and full read/write access to the application's data. This is the standard preliminary to a database MITM, not a theoretical one.
findings.recommendation: Ship the provider's CA and pass it: ssl: { ca: fs.readFileSync(process.env.PGSSLROOTCERT), rejectUnauthorized: true }.

findings.title: SQL injection in the retained rollup helper
findings.evidence: WHERE tenant = '${tenantName}' interpolated into pool.query with no parameter array. The function is exported (db.js:58) but grep finds no caller in this tree, and the comment at db.js:46-47 says a nightly job still expects it.
findings.impact: Not reachable from any resolver as shipped. Because the call passes no parameter array, node-postgres uses the simple query protocol, which permits multiple statements separated by ';' - so whichever job does call it turns a tenant name into arbitrary SQL execution, not merely data disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Parameterise it (WHERE tenant = $1) whether or not the caller is retired, or delete the export.

findings.title: Server-side template injection from a request-supplied Jinja2 template
findings.evidence: handler reads payload['inlineTemplate'] straight from the request body and passes it to _render_inline, which is Template(source).render(**ctx) - the request body becomes the template, not the data. No sandbox (jinja2.sandbox.SandboxedEnvironment) is used. It is also the documented bypass of the TEMPLATE_REGISTRY allowlist in common/config.py:15-21, whose comment claims 'A request that names anything outside this table is rejected before a path is built'; inlineTemplate never consults the table.
findings.impact: Jinja2 template expressions reach Python attributes, so this is arbitrary code execution in the Lambda: read /proc/self/environ for MAILROOM_SIGNING_SECRET (template.yaml:29) and the function's AWS credentials, then use the role. The endpoint that reaches it needs no credential at all (template.yaml:107-108).
findings.recommendation: Remove _render_inline, or compile customer snippets in a SandboxedEnvironment with autoescape=True, no attribute access, and a per-workspace authorization check before the snippet is accepted.

findings.title: Render function published on a Lambda function URL with no authentication
findings.evidence: AuthType: NONE under RenderFunction's FunctionUrlConfig. The Cors block below it names https://app.mailroom.example, which constrains browsers only - a function URL with AuthType NONE answers any caller on the internet, and handlers/render.py performs no authentication or authorization of its own.
findings.impact: Every defect in render.py is reachable pre-authentication: the template injection above and the arbitrary object read below. It also gives anyone an unmetered invoke path into the account's Lambda.
findings.recommendation: Set AuthType: AWS_IAM (or front the function with API Gateway plus an authorizer) and have the handler verify the caller's workspace before it touches the store.

findings.title: Arbitrary object read from the mail store via the request's messageKey
findings.evidence: message_key = payload.get('messageKey') is checked only for truthiness (render.py:59-61) and then handed to storage.get_object (common/storage.py:26-28) as the S3 Key with no prefix, no ownership lookup and no format check. Its content is returned to the caller inside the rendered HTML via ctx['body'] (render.py:66) and the 200 response (render.py:78).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller reads any object in MAIL_BUCKET by naming it - raw/<messageId>.eml is every stored message, raw/callbacks/* is every delivery record - which is the entire mail archive of every tenant. The bucket's public-access block and KMS encryption do not apply, because the read is performed by the function's own credentials.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the key server-side from an identifier scoped to the authenticated caller, or at minimum require the key to match a strict per-tenant prefix pattern and verify ownership before get_object.

findings.title: Unsigned delivery callbacks are accepted as valid
findings.evidence: verify_signature returns True when the X-Mailroom-Signature header is absent (webhook.py:44-49) - the only rejection paths are a malformed header and a bad digest, so the control cannot fail for a caller who simply omits the header. handler treats its return as the gate (webhook.py:71-72). tests/test_webhook.py exercises round-trip, wrong secret and stale timestamp, and never the missing-header case, so the suite is green over the hole.
findings.impact: Anyone who finds the API Gateway URL POSTs arbitrary delivery state for any message id: state transitions are recorded to the store as authentic (webhook.py:83-93) with a chosen messageId, so delivery history can be forged or flooded without any credential.
findings.recommendation: Return False when the header is missing. If a carrier truly needs an unsigned onboarding period, gate it on an explicit per-carrier flag that defaults to off and cannot be set in the prod stage.

findings.title: Webhook signing secret committed in the SAM template
findings.evidence: MAILROOM_SIGNING_SECRET: mrs_7d41c0a9e2b84f60a1c35de8f9b21047 written as a literal under Globals, so it is injected into all three functions. The comment above it confirms it is the live shared value ('the delivery partner signs callbacks with the same value'), and the same file already grants secretsmanager access to the inbound function, so the mechanism to avoid this exists in the stack.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository access can sign callbacks that verify_signature accepts, which is the only integrity control on the callback endpoint; the value is also visible to anyone with lambda:GetFunctionConfiguration on any of the three functions. It must be considered compromised from the moment it was committed.
findings.recommendation: Move it to Secrets Manager or an SSM SecureString, reference it at runtime, rotate the current value with the carrier, and scrub it from the git history.

findings.title: Autoescaping is configured but does not apply to the templates that are rendered
findings.evidence: The Environment is built with autoescape=select_autoescape(['html','xml','j2']) (render.py:18-21), but _render_named reads the file itself and calls _env.from_string(fh.read()). select_autoescape decides from a template name; from_string supplies none, so the default_for_string branch applies and escaping is off. The FileSystemLoader configured on line 19 is never used - nothing in the module calls _env.get_template - which is the tell that the name-based rule never gets a name.
findings.impact: ctx['body'] is the raw stored message (render.py:66) - content any outsider can put there by sending mail - and subject/recipient come straight from the request. All three land unescaped in HTML that the reader pane displays, so this is stored XSS in the web app, on a path the code is written to believe is escaped.
findings.recommendation: Render through the loader (_env.get_template(filename).render(**ctx)) so the .j2 name triggers the rule, or pass autoescape=True explicitly; and pass default_for_string=True to select_autoescape so any from_string path is safe by default.

findings.title: Attachment filenames are joined into a path without sanitisation
findings.evidence: target = os.path.join(config.TMP_ROOT, filename) with filename arriving from part.get_filename() (handlers/inbound.py:42-46) and from pointer['name'] (inbound.py:61). No basename call, no normalisation, no containment check; os.path.join returns the second argument unchanged when it is absolute, and does not collapse '..'. The docstring states the original filename is kept deliberately.
findings.impact: A MIME part named ../../something or /tmp/other/path writes outside /tmp/mailroom - inside the function's writable space it can overwrite files the virus scanner and thumbnailer named in the docstring are about to read, and clear_scratch (storage.py:47-52) will not clean what escaped its walk root.
findings.recommendation: Derive the on-disk name from a server-side value (a uuid, or sha256 of the content) and keep only a validated extension; if the original name must survive, use os.path.basename and assert os.path.realpath(target).startswith(os.path.realpath(TMP_ROOT) + os.sep).

findings.title: Inbound function granted s3:* and secretsmanager:* on every resource
findings.evidence: Action: ['s3:*','secretsmanager:*'] with Resource: '*' and no Condition. The two sibling functions in the same file use scoped SAM policy templates - S3ReadPolicy/S3WritePolicy bound to !Ref MailStore (template.yaml:105-106, 122-123) - so the wildcard is an outlier in this stack, not a house convention.
findings.impact: The function that parses untrusted email content is also the one that can read and delete every bucket in the account and read every secret in it. Any code-execution or SSRF foothold in inbound.py escalates immediately to account-wide data access, and secretsmanager:* includes writes as well as GetSecretValue.
findings.recommendation: Replace with the same scoped templates the siblings use: S3WritePolicy on MailStore plus, if a secret really is needed, an explicit secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on that one secret's ARN.

findings.title: eval() on a queue payload in the retained reprocessing path
findings.evidence: note = eval(queue_body) where queue_body is described in the comment above as 'a python literal of the SES event' taken off the old queue. grep finds no caller inside this tree, and the comment says the replay tooling that used it is being rewritten.
findings.impact: Anything that can place a message on the legacy queue executes arbitrary Python in the Lambda, with that function's s3:*/secretsmanager:* role. Not reachable from the three declared handlers as shipped, which is why it is medium rather than high.
findings.recommendation: Use ast.literal_eval if a Python literal really must be parsed, or json.loads once the producer is converted; delete the function with the replay tool.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled filename written into the log without neutralisation
findings.evidence: log.info('staged attachment %s (%d bytes)', target, len(body)) - target embeds the unmodified MIME filename from inbound.py:42-46. The corpus enumerator (tools/log_escaper.py) flags exactly this line as UNCLEARED and clears only the literal-argument call in webhook.py:48; there is no escaper on the path and the deferred %s form does not provide one.
findings.impact: A filename containing CRLF plus a plausible record makes one attachment produce two CloudWatch entries, so an outsider who can send mail can forge log lines, break prefix-matching alert rules and destroy the audit trail for the ingestion path. Impact stops short of execution unless a viewer renders the line as HTML, which cannot be established from this tree.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise before logging - filename.encode('unicode_escape').decode() or a strict [A-Za-z0-9._-] filter - or emit one JSON object per event and confirm the consumer parses that format.

findings.title: Attachment URL from the notification is fetched with no allowlist
findings.evidence: SESSION.get(url, timeout=10, stream=True) where url is note['attachmentUrls'][i]['url'], taken from the SNS message body (inbound.py:22-23, 59-60). No scheme or host allowlist, and redirects are followed by default in requests.
findings.impact: A URL pointing at 169.254.169.254 or any VPC-internal address is fetched from the function's network position and its response is written to /tmp. The precondition is control over the notification body: the topic (template.yaml:74-77) carries no explicit publish policy, so the default account-only policy applies and the producer is SES - and attachmentUrls is not a field SES emits. That is why this is reported low and as a hardening gap rather than a live path; it would settle by seeing the real producer.
findings.recommendation: Validate the URL against the expected host before fetching, disable redirects (allow_redirects=False), and re-check the resolved address is not link-local or private.

findings.title: The 25 MB attachment ceiling is enforced on one ingestion path and not its sibling
findings.evidence: config.MAX_ATTACHMENT_BYTES is read exactly once in the tree, in _fetch_remote_attachment (inbound.py:31-33) for URL-borne attachments. _store_parts writes part.get_payload(decode=True) to disk with no size check at all (inbound.py:45-46), and the loop has no cap on the number of parts either.
findings.impact: A message with large or numerous MIME parts fills the function's writable scratch space, failing the ingestion of that and any concurrent message on the same execution environment; the declared ceiling gives the reader the impression the path is bounded when only half of it is.
findings.recommendation: Apply the same ceiling in _store_parts (and a part count cap), or move the check into storage.stage_attachment so both callers inherit it.

findings.title: Order lookup by id is not scoped to the caller's organisation
findings.evidence: get(@PathVariable long id) calls orders.findById(id) - the repository method with no tenant predicate (OrderRepository.java:44-48). Its sibling findByIdAndOrgId exists on line 51 with the comment 'Same lookup, but scoped to the organisation the caller belongs to', and update (line 72) and note (line 87) both use it. get is also the only handler in the class that does not take a CallerContext parameter, so it never resolves the caller at all.
findings.impact: Any caller of the API reads any order in the ledger by incrementing the id: customer reference, total, currency, shipping address and internal_note (mapped at OrderRepository.java:29-42) for every organisation. This is the asymmetry decidable inside one file - the gate exists on the siblings and is absent here.
findings.recommendation: Take CallerContext and call findByIdAndOrgId(id, caller.orgId()), returning 404 on a miss so ids stay unenumerable.

findings.title: XML feed parsed with entity expansion enabled and no secure processing
findings.evidence: DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() followed by factory.setExpandEntityReferences(true) and nothing else: no FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, no http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl, no external-general-entities/external-parameter-entities set to false, no setXIncludeAware(false), no EntityResolver. The document parsed on line 46 is the raw request body bound at OrderController.java:109.
findings.impact: A feed carrying a DOCTYPE with an external entity makes the server read local files (the parsed value lands in customerRef/shippingAddress and comes back through the ledger) and issue requests from its own network position to internal hosts. The comment on lines 40-42 shows entity expansion was turned on deliberately for shared country/currency tables, which is exactly the configuration that enables it.
findings.recommendation: Set disallow-doctype-decl to true, or if a DTD is genuinely required, set FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING plus external-general-entities and external-parameter-entities to false and setXIncludeAware(false); resolve the shared tables locally rather than through entities.

findings.title: Imported orders are written by client-supplied id with no tenant predicate
findings.evidence: order.setId(Long.parseLong(text(element,"id"))) takes the row id from the feed, and orders.update(order) issues UPDATE orders SET ... WHERE id = ? (OrderRepository.java:76-88) - the only write in the repository with no org_id in its WHERE clause. setOrgId(orgId) on line 57 sets a field the UPDATE statement never uses, so the caller's organisation constrains nothing.
findings.impact: A feed that names another organisation's order id overwrites that row's customer reference, status, total, currency, shipping address and internal note. Ledger records of other tenants can be silently rewritten - a total set to 0 or a status set to DELIVERED - through an endpoint whose documented purpose is importing one's own day of orders.
findings.recommendation: Add org_id to the predicate (UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND org_id = ?), assert the affected-row count, and treat the feed's id as a customer reference to be matched rather than as a primary key.

findings.title: H2 console enabled in the default profile, permitted without authentication and open to remote hosts
findings.evidence: spring.h2.console.enabled: true with settings.web-allow-others: true sits in the unprofiled top document, which is the one active under spring.profiles.active: prod (line 5); the local override at line 63 changes only the datasource and CORS. SecurityConfig.java:70 then adds requestMatchers(toH2Console()).permitAll(), and line 67 relaxes frameOptions to sameOrigin so the console's frames render. com.h2database is a runtime dependency of the build (pom.xml:47-51), so the auto-configuration activates.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller reaches /h2-console and supplies any JDBC URL of its choosing. That is direct interactive database access, and H2's own facilities (RUNSCRIPT, CREATE ALIAS) make it a code-execution surface on the application host. It is the only application path in this service reachable with no credential at all.
findings.recommendation: Delete the spring.h2.console block from the default document (keep it only under the local profile), drop the toH2Console() permitAll rule, and move the h2 dependency to test scope.

findings.title: Database password committed in the production configuration
findings.evidence: password: 0rd3rb00k-app-2024 as a literal beside url: jdbc:postgresql://orderbook-db.internal:5432/orderbook and username: orderbook_app, in the document that is active under the prod profile. No ${...} placeholder and no environment indirection, in contrast to the JWT key, which SecurityConfig.java:50-53 reads from ORDERBOOK_JWT_KEY and refuses to start without.
findings.impact: Everyone with repository or artifact access holds the production database credential for the orderbook_app account. It must be treated as compromised, and the exposure is compounded by the actuator finding below, which serves the same value back over HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Replace with ${DB_PASSWORD} sourced from the deployment's secret store, rotate the credential, and remove it from the git history.

findings.title: All actuator endpoints exposed to any authenticated caller
findings.evidence: include: "*" exposes the full actuator surface under /actuator. SecurityConfig.java:69 permits only health and info anonymously and leaves the rest to anyRequest().authenticated() - so every other endpoint (env, configprops, beans, mappings, threaddump, heapdump, loggers) is reachable by any caller the service accepts, with no role condition anywhere.
findings.impact: /actuator/env and /actuator/configprops return spring.datasource.password from application.yml:9; /actuator/heapdump returns process memory, which contains the JWT signing key loaded at SecurityConfig.java:54. A single low-privilege account therefore yields the database credential and the ability to mint tokens. /actuator/loggers additionally allows changing log levels at runtime.
findings.recommendation: Expose only what is needed (include: health,info,prometheus), and require a management role for anything beyond that: requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()).hasRole("OPS").

findings.title: Order update binds the request body onto the entity with no field allowlist or state-machine check
findings.evidence: @RequestBody Order incoming binds the persistence model directly; only id and orgId are restored from the looked-up row (lines 74-75). Everything else the client sends is written by OrderRepository.update: customerRef, status, totalCents, currency, shippingAddress and internalNote. OrderStatus.isTerminal() (model/OrderStatus.java:17-19) exists to describe a terminal state and has no caller anywhere in the tree, so no transition is validated.
findings.impact: Any caller who can update an order in their own organisation sets its totalCents to an arbitrary value, rewrites internalNote (a staff field the UI does not offer) and moves status backwards out of DELIVERED or CANCELLED. In a fulfilment ledger these are the values the business runs on.
findings.recommendation: Bind a DTO carrying only the fields the console may edit, keep status changes behind an explicit transition method that consults isTerminal(), and treat totalCents and internalNote as server-owned.

findings.title: The token's roles claim is never enforced, and the OPS gate rests on authorities nothing populates
findings.evidence: hasRole("OPS") guards /api/orders/export and /api/orders/import (lines 71-72), which requires a ROLE_OPS authority on the Spring Security Authentication. Nothing in this tree establishes one: there is no authentication filter, no AuthenticationProvider and no UserDetailsService (grep for OncePerRequestFilter, addFilter, httpBasic, formLogin returns nothing). The token is parsed instead by an argument resolver at controller-invocation time (lines 115-131), and the roles it extracts into CallerContext (line 93) have exactly one other occurrence in the tree - the record declaration on line 134. No handler reads caller.roles().
findings.impact: Function-level authorization for the two staff-only routes is decoupled from the credential the service actually validates: the claim that names a caller as OPS is parsed and discarded, and the rule that names the requirement is written against a principal no component in this configuration builds. As declared the chain fails closed, but any change that supplies an Authentication - a second filter chain, a gateway-populated principal - grants export and import on whatever authorities that mechanism happens to carry, not on the token's roles.
findings.recommendation: Establish the principal in a filter that runs the same Jwts.parser() validation and maps the roles claim to granted authorities, so hasRole("OPS") and CallerContext derive from one verified source; add a test that calls export and import with a non-OPS token and expects 403.

findings.title: Retained JWT parser that reads claims without verifying the signature
findings.evidence: Jwts.parser().build().parseUnsecuredClaims(payload) after splitting the token and base64-decoding part [1] - no verifyWith, no issuer or audience requirement, in contrast to resolve() ten lines above. Marked @Deprecated with a comment saying the console it served no longer exists; grep finds no caller.
findings.impact: Not reachable as shipped. It is a package-private method returning a fully-formed CallerContext from an attacker-writable payload, so any future wiring of it - or a test that exercises it against production data - hands out a principal of the caller's choosing.
findings.recommendation: Delete it; the gateway it was written for was retired.

findings.title: Every website may drive the extension's privileged commands
findings.evidence: externally_connectable.matches is ['*://*/*'], so any page on any origin can call chrome.runtime.sendMessage(<extensionId>, msg). background.js:54-57 registers onMessageExternal and forwards straight into handle(message) - the same function the trusted popup uses (line 47) - without looking at sender.origin, sender.url or sender.id. handle() has no per-command origin condition either (lines 17-45).
findings.impact: An arbitrary web page issues 'annotate' with a note of its choosing, which reaches the content script's innerHTML sink in every page the user has open (see next finding), and issues 'push' with a clip body of its choosing, which lib/sync.js:22-34 sends to the workspace API under the user's stored bearer token - a confused-deputy write with the victim's credential. 'capture' additionally attempts a screenshot of the active tab, which succeeds on any tab where activeTab has already been granted by the user clicking the action.
findings.recommendation: Narrow externally_connectable.matches to the workspace origins only, and additionally check sender.origin against that list at the top of the onMessageExternal listener; keep the privileged commands (capture, push) on the internal onMessage channel.

findings.title: Message-supplied note inserted into every page as HTML
findings.evidence:
node.innerHTML = `Note
${note}
` with note taken from the message (content.js:51). The only sanitisation in the extension is in the popup - escapeHtml plus markdownLite at popup.js:5-12 and 69-74 - applied before the message is sent (popup.js:42), not at the sink. The content script is injected into (manifest.json:27-33), so the sink exists on every page.
findings.impact: Any sender that can reach the background worker - which, per the previous finding, is every website - injects script into whatever page is active. Because content scripts run in an isolated world the injected markup executes in the page's own context, so this is cross-site scripting against arbitrary third-party origins: it reads and acts on the victim's session on whichever site is open.
findings.recommendation: Build the bubble with DOM calls and textContent, or sanitise at the sink; the popup's escaping is not a control for messages the popup did not send.

findings.title: The debugger permission is requested and never used
findings.evidence: 'debugger' is listed among the permissions; grep across background.js, content.js, popup.js, lib/sync.js and lib/allowlist.js finds no chrome.debugger call. The capture path uses chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab (background.js:6) and needs nothing from it.
findings.impact: chrome.debugger attaches the Chrome DevTools Protocol to any tab: it reads and writes any page's DOM, cookies and network traffic regardless of host permissions. Granting it enlarges the blast radius of every other defect in this extension - the externally reachable message channel above becomes a path to a component that holds full CDP rights - and it is the permission most likely to draw a supply-chain attacker to this extension.
findings.recommendation: Remove 'debugger' from the manifest; nothing in the shipped code consumes it.

findings.title: All extension resources exposed to all web pages
findings.evidence: resources: ['*'] with matches: ['<all_urls>'] - every file in the package, including background.js, lib/sync.js and lib/allowlist.js, is fetchable by any page. Nothing in the tree loads an extension URL from a page context, so no resource actually needs to be listed.
findings.impact: Any site can fetch the extension's source to fingerprint the installed version and read its endpoints and constants, and the entry no longer restricts which origins may do so. It also removes the resource-level barrier that would otherwise limit what a page can pull out of the package.
findings.recommendation: Replace with the specific files that must be page-reachable - if there are none, remove the key entirely - and scope matches to the workspace origins.

findings.title: Retained upload helper posts clips over plaintext HTTP to a caller-supplied host
findings.evidence: fetch(`http://${host}/v1/clips`, ...) - the scheme is hard-coded http and host is a parameter. grep finds no caller; the comment on lines 42-45 says the self-hosted appliance it served has been replaced and it goes away at the next manifest bump.
findings.impact: Not reachable as shipped. If wired up again it transmits captured screenshots - which are whatever was on screen - in the clear to a host taken from settings, and unlike pushClip it does not read or attach the auth token, so there is not even an authenticated channel to notice the change.
findings.recommendation: Delete it with the manifest bump the comment promises.

findings.title: Application container runs privileged
findings.evidence: securityContext: privileged: true with readOnlyRootFilesystem: false, and no runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, allowPrivilegeEscalation or capabilities.drop anywhere in the pod or container context (the pod-level block at lines 32-33 sets only fsGroup). The value is a template literal, not a chart value, so no values override can turn it off.
findings.impact: A privileged container holds all capabilities and can access host devices; combined with the Docker socket mounted into the same container it is equivalent to root on the node, and from there on every workload scheduled there. It also nullifies any restricted Pod Security Admission expectation for the namespace.
findings.recommendation: Remove privileged, set runAsNonRoot: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true and capabilities.drop: [ALL]; if the snapshotter genuinely needs a capability, add that one capability to a dedicated sidecar rather than privileging the application.

findings.title: Host Docker socket mounted into the application pod
findings.evidence: hostPath: path: /var/run/docker.sock, type: Socket, mounted at /var/run/docker.sock in the ledger container (lines 80-83), gated on reconciler.mountDockerSocket which values.yaml:48 sets to true by default. The comment at values.yaml:46-47 explains the nightly job snapshots the container filesystem through the node's daemon.
findings.impact: Write access to the Docker socket is root on the node: a caller can start a container with the host filesystem mounted and no restrictions, read every other pod's secrets from the kubelet directory, and pivot across the cluster. It is granted here to the long-running web-facing pod, not just to the nightly job that needs it.
findings.recommendation: Default mountDockerSocket to false and take the snapshot with a mechanism that does not require the daemon socket (a CSI snapshot, or a node-scoped job with its own tightly bound service account); never mount it into the pod serving ingress traffic.

findings.title: Operator account password hard-coded in the pod environment
findings.evidence: - name: LEDGER_ADMIN_PASSWORD / value: "r3conc1le-op-2024!" as a plain value, two entries below LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD, which does the same job correctly with valueFrom.secretKeyRef (lines 57-61). The comment above it says the value bootstraps 'the built-in operator account the reconciler signs in with before the platform IdP is reachable'.
findings.impact: The credential for a built-in administrative account is in the chart, so it is in the repository, in every rendered manifest, in the Deployment object readable by anyone with get on deployments in the namespace, and in the environment of a privileged container. It must be treated as compromised, and it grants an account whose whole purpose is to work when the IdP does not.
findings.recommendation: Move it into the same secret as the database password and reference it with secretKeyRef, rotate the value, and prefer a short-lived bootstrap credential the reconciler exchanges rather than a static one.

findings.title: Upstream TLS certificate verification disabled by default
findings.evidence: insecureSkipTLSVerify: true is the chart default and is passed to the workload as LEDGER_UPSTREAM_INSECURE (deployment.yaml:53-54). The comment at lines 31-33 says the clearing house presents a certificate signed by its own CA and that shipping that root into the image was avoided.
findings.impact: The connection to https://clearing.partner.example is encrypted but unauthenticated, so anyone who can intercept or redirect that route presents their own certificate and is trusted - and this is the hop carrying clearing traffic and the clearing-token held in the chart's secret. The stated problem (a private CA) has a solution that does not involve disabling verification.
findings.recommendation: Mount the partner CA bundle from a ConfigMap and point the client at it, then set insecureSkipTLSVerify to false as the chart default.

findings.title: Break-glass pod spec with host namespaces and a full host mount retained in the chart
findings.evidence: The define block sets hostPID: true, hostNetwork: true, privileged: true, runAsUser: 0 and mounts hostPath / at /host. The comment at lines 17-20 says the job it belonged to was dropped in 2.4 and that no template renders it; grep confirms the only occurrence of breakGlassPodSpec in the tree is this definition.
findings.impact: Nothing renders it today, so it creates no live exposure. It is a ready-made node-takeover pod spec that a single {{ include }} line would activate, sitting in the file a chart author edits most, and it is invisible to any scanner that only reads rendered output.
findings.recommendation: Delete it; the runbook diff belongs in version history, not in a template helper the chart can include.
